scenarios.title: Print a reliable handover
scenarios.summary: Use variables and quoted output to create a dependable handover.
scenarios.objective: Print exactly two lines: Site: followed by SITE, then Task: followed by TASK, with one space after each colon. Keep spaces and literal percent signs in the values.

guide.title: Understand the task
guide.why: Each test starts with its own sample inputs. Simulated files reset before each test. Inspect the inputs and expected results.
guide.action: Use the case selector to inspect inputs, then edit the script.

guide.title: Make the behavior reliable
guide.why: Quoted expansions preserve spaces and empty data. printf treats percent signs in a %s argument as ordinary data, not a new format.
guide.action: Run script executes every case. Inspect the output and specific failing check, edit, and retry.

guide.title: Explain the edge cases
guide.why: A script that works once can still fail on spaces, missing files or empty data.
guide.action: Compare the cases. Why does the same script handle every input?

scenarios.explanation:
Quoted expansions preserve spaces and empty data. printf treats percent signs in a %s argument as ordinary data, not a new format.

One supported solution:
site=$SITE
printf 'Site: %s\nTask: %s\n' "$site" "$TASK"
hints: The lab supplies SITE and TASK. Read their values as "$SITE" and "$TASK"; create your own named value with name=value if useful.
Double quotes keep each expanded value together. printf separates the fixed format from the data.
A format such as printf 'Site: %s\n' "$SITE" prints one complete line.

teaching.prerequisite_note: Start here: no shell knowledge is needed.

concepts.title: A script is a saved set of instructions
concepts.text: Type instructions in the script editor. Run reads them from top to bottom and shows what they print. Here it runs only in the offline simulator; it cannot change your computer.

concepts.title: Comments and printed text
concepts.text: A line starting with # is a comment: a note that is not run. printf prints text. A command name comes first, followed by the information it needs, separated by spaces.

concepts.title: Variables are names for values
concepts.text: visitor='Mina' creates a variable named visitor; use no spaces around =. "$visitor" reads its value. The example also has ROOM, supplied by the lab before Run. You create visitor; you do not create ROOM. In the assignment, SITE and TASK are supplied instead.

concepts.title: Quotes and printf formatting
concepts.text: Single quotes keep the format text literal. In double quotes, $visitor is replaced by its value and kept together, even with spaces. In printf, %s means “insert the next text value here”; \n (backslash then n) means “start a new line.” The format and the values are separate pieces.

teaching.example:
# A comment is a note, not an instruction.
visitor='Mina'
printf 'Welcome\n'
printf 'Hello, %s!\n' "$visitor"
printf 'Room: %s\n' "$ROOM"
teaching.inputs: ROOM is supplied as Library. This example has no arguments, input text or files.
teaching.try_change: Change Mina to Rowan, then Run example again. The greeting should change; the room should stay Library.

scenarios.summary: Turn positional arguments into a clear, reusable report.
scenarios.objective: Read label from argument 1 and a file path from argument 2. Print Label: LABEL and File: PATH on separate lines. Preserve both arguments exactly, including spaces and an empty label.

guide.action: Use the case selector to inspect inputs, then edit the script.

guide.title: Make the behavior reliable
guide.why: Arguments are data. Saving them in named variables makes intent readable, and quoting their later expansion keeps file names with spaces intact.
guide.action: Run script executes every case. Inspect the output and specific failing check, edit, and retry.

guide.title: Explain the edge cases
guide.why: A script that works once can still fail on spaces, missing files or empty data.
guide.action: Compare the cases. Why does the same script handle every input?

scenarios.explanation:
Arguments are data. Saving them in named variables makes intent readable, and quoting their later expansion keeps file names with spaces intact.

One supported solution:

file=$2
printf 'Label: %s\nFile: %s\n' "$label" "$file"
hints: $1 and $2 refer to the arguments, not file contents.
A line such as label=$1 saves argument 1 under a name you choose. Later, quote "$label" when passing it to printf.
Use one %s placeholder for each value rather than using the value as the format.

concepts.title: Arguments are values passed to a script
concepts.text: An argument is a separate piece of information given when Run starts the script. $1 reads the first argument and $2 the second. They are supplied values, like the lab variables you used earlier, but identified by position.

concepts.title: Give those values useful names

scenarios.title: Read a request without losing backslashes
scenarios.summary: Read finite input and distinguish data from escape characters.
scenarios.objective: Read one line from standard input into request with read -r. Print Request: VALUE and a newline. Use normal default whitespace trimming; keep internal spaces and literal backslashes.

guide.title: Understand the task
guide.why: Each test starts with its own sample inputs. Simulated files reset before each test. Inspect the inputs and expected results.
guide.action: Use the case selector to inspect inputs, then edit the script.

guide.title: Make the behavior reliable
guide.why: read -r disables backslash interpretation. With one variable and the default whitespace separators, outer spaces/tabs are trimmed while internal spacing remains.
guide.action: Run script executes every case. Inspect the output and specific failing check, edit, and retry.

guide.title: Explain the edge cases
guide.why: A script that works once can still fail on spaces, missing files or empty data.
guide.action: Compare the cases. Why does the same script handle every input?

scenarios.explanation:
read -r disables backslash interpretation. With one variable and the default whitespace separators, outer spaces/tabs are trimmed while internal spacing remains.

One supported solution:
read -r request
printf 'Request: %s\n' "$request"
hints: read consumes standard input; it does not read the argument list.
Use read -r request so backslashes stay literal.
Quote "$request" when printing, so its internal spaces survive.

initial.source: # Standard input contains one request line.

teaching.prerequisite_note: Builds on labs 1–2: quoted values and the difference between script text and supplied arguments.

concepts.title: Input and output are different directions
concepts.text: Standard input is text supplied for a running script to read. Standard output is the normal text it prints. Arguments are separate starting values; read does not read the argument list. The simulator supplies input text, so it will not wait for your keyboard.

concepts.title: Read one line into a variable
concepts.text: read -r note reads one line and creates or updates note. The -r option keeps backslashes as ordinary characters. With one variable, this form removes spaces and tabs at the ends but keeps spaces inside the line. Print "$note" to keep those internal spaces.

concepts.title: What is a line break?
concepts.text: A line break ends a line. printf uses \n to print one. A backslash in input, such as the one in C:\plans, is data, not a request to print a line break.

teaching.inputs: Input text: two spaces, Meet  at C:\plans, two spaces, then a line break. No arguments are supplied.
teaching.try_change: Change Note: to Reminder: and Run. The two spaces between Meet and at should remain.

scenarios.title: Reject a missing destination
scenarios.summary: Use a condition and exit status to make failure visible.
scenarios.objective: If argument 1 is empty or missing, print Destination required to standard error and exit 2. Otherwise print Destination: VALUE to standard output and exit 0. Do not change files.

guide.title: Understand the task
guide.why: Each test starts with its own sample inputs. Simulated files reset before each test. Inspect the inputs and expected results.
guide.action: Use the case selector to inspect inputs, then edit the script.

guide.title: Make the behavior reliable
guide.why: Shell conditions inspect exit status: zero means true/success. A guard gives a useful diagnostic on standard error and stops before normal output. Keeping errors separate helps callers.
guide.action: Run script executes every case. Inspect the output and specific failing check, edit, and retry.

guide.title: Explain the edge cases
guide.why: A script that works once can still fail on spaces, missing files or empty data.
guide.action: Compare the cases. Why does the same script handle every input?

scenarios.explanation:
Shell conditions inspect exit status: zero means true/success. A guard gives a useful diagnostic on standard error and stops before normal output. Keeping errors separate helps callers.

One supported solution:
if [ -z "$1" ]; then
    printf 'Destination required\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
printf 'Destination: %s\n' "$1"
hints: [ -z "$1" ] succeeds when the first argument is empty. Spaces around [ and ] matter.
An if runs its then block when the condition returns status 0.
>&2 sends the message to standard error. exit 2 ends the script with a deliberate failure status.
scenarios.simplifications: Shell subset v1, documented in Help. UTF-8 virtual /work files; no host processes or files. Each test starts with its own sample inputs and resets the simulated files. All syntax in this introductory unit is portable shell; Bash-specific features are planned separately.

teaching.prerequisite_note: Builds on labs 1–3: arguments, quotes, printed output and supplied input.

concepts.title: Commands report whether they succeeded
concepts.text: An exit status is a number a command returns: 0 means success; other numbers report another outcome. The script normally returns its last command’s status. exit 2 stops it immediately and returns 2.

concepts.title: Choose what runs with a condition
concepts.text: [ -z "$1" ] tests whether argument 1 is empty or missing. -n tests the opposite: whether text is non-empty. Keep spaces after [ and before ]. if runs the then instructions when the test succeeds (status 0); else gives another path. fi ends the choice. A ; can separate instructions where a new line would also work.

concepts.title: Keep problems separate from normal output
concepts.text: Standard error is a second output channel for problem messages. >&2 sends a printf message there instead of to normal output. A guard is an early check that explains a problem and stops before doing other work.

teaching.example:
if [ -z "$1" ]; then
    printf 'Name needed\n' >&2
    exit 2
else
    printf 'Hello, %s\n' "$1"
fi
teaching.inputs: No arguments are supplied, so the example takes the missing-name path. The message belongs in Standard error.
teaching.try_change: Change -z to -n, which tests for a non-empty value. Run again with the same empty input and observe the other path.

scenarios.title: Write an incident report
scenarios.summary: Filter virtual data and direct output into a report file.
scenarios.objective: Argument 1 names an input log; argument 2 names the report. Write exactly the lines containing the literal ERROR to the report, replacing any old report. Leave input and other files unchanged. Print nothing. Return grep’s status: 0 for matches, 1 for none. Inputs always exist.

guide.title: Understand the task
guide.why: Each test starts with its own sample inputs. Simulated files reset before each test. Inspect the inputs and expected results.
guide.action: Use the case selector to inspect inputs, then edit the script.

guide.title: Make the behavior reliable
guide.why: Redirection opens or truncates the destination before grep runs. grep returns 1 when no lines match; that is a meaningful outcome rather than a syntax error. The final command supplies the script’s status.
guide.action: Run script executes every case. Inspect the output and specific failing check, edit, and retry.

guide.title: Explain the edge cases
guide.why: A script that works once can still fail on spaces, missing files or empty data.
guide.action: Compare the cases. Why does the same script handle every input?

scenarios.explanation:
Redirection opens or truncates the destination before grep runs. grep returns 1 when no lines match; that is a meaningful outcome rather than a syntax error. The final command supplies the script’s status.

One supported solution:
grep -F ERROR "$1" > "$2"
hints: grep -F matches literal text, one line at a time.
> redirects standard output and replaces a previous report; >> would append.
Quote both paths. A no-match status of 1 is expected for the sample with no matching lines.

concepts.title: A path names a virtual file
concepts.text: A file contains text; its path is its name in the simulated workspace. /work/visitors names the example input. A path argument is just a name until a command opens that file. These files never refer to your computer’s files.

concepts.title: Select lines with grep
concepts.text: grep -F OPEN "$1" reads the file named by argument 1 and prints each line containing the literal text OPEN. -F means ordinary text, not a special search pattern. Letter case matters. grep returns 0 if it finds lines, 1 if it finds none, or 2 for a read problem.

concepts.title: Send output to a file
concepts.text: > "$2" sends normal output to the file named by argument 2 instead of the output display. It creates that file or replaces its previous contents, before the command runs. >> would add to the end instead. Run starts with fresh example files each time.

teaching.inputs: Arguments: /work/visitors and /work/open-list. The input contains OPEN Mina, CLOSED Dev and OPEN Rowan on separate lines.
teaching.try_change: Change OPEN to CLOSED and Run again. Inspect the example files below the output to see the different report.

OPEN Mina
CLOSED Dev
OPEN Rowan

OPEN Mina
CLOSED Dev

scenarios.title: Assemble a file handover
scenarios.summary: Loop over a variable number of files without splitting their names.
scenarios.objective: For each path argument, in order, print File: PATH and then its contents. All supplied files exist and end in a newline. Preserve spaces and argument order; with no arguments print nothing. Do not change files.

guide.title: Understand the task
guide.why: Each test starts with its own sample inputs. Simulated files reset before each test. Inspect the inputs and expected results.
guide.action: Use the case selector to inspect inputs, then edit the script.

guide.title: Make the behavior reliable
guide.why: Sole quoted "$@" expands to one word per positional argument. With no arguments it supplies zero words, so the loop runs zero times. This prevents spaces in names becoming extra iterations.
guide.action: Run script executes every case. Inspect the output and specific failing check, edit, and retry.

guide.title: Explain the edge cases
guide.why: A script that works once can still fail on spaces, missing files or empty data.
guide.action: Compare the cases. Why does the same script handle every input?

scenarios.explanation:
Sole quoted "$@" expands to one word per positional argument. With no arguments it supplies zero words, so the loop runs zero times. This prevents spaces in names becoming extra iterations.

One supported solution:
for file in "$@"; do
    printf 'File: %s\n' "$file"
    cat "$file"
done
hints: for file in "$@" iterates over the original argument boundaries.
Inside the loop, quote "$file" for both the heading and cat.
Keep the print and cat inside do … done so each heading stays next to its contents.

solution:
for file in "$@"; do

teaching.prerequisite_note: Builds on lab 5: file paths, quoted arguments and printed reports.

concepts.title: Repeat a group of instructions
concepts.text: A for loop repeats its do … done instructions once for each supplied value. for path in "$@" gives path each original argument in order. "$@" means all arguments, keeping spaces and empty arguments intact. With no arguments, there is nothing to repeat.

concepts.title: Read the contents of each file
concepts.text: cat "$path" prints the file’s text. It does not print the name, so printf can put a heading before it. The loop variable path is created by for; you read its current value as "$path". Put both commands inside do … done to keep each heading beside its text.

teaching.example:
for path in "$@"; do
    printf 'Reading %s\n' "$path"
    cat "$path"
done
teaching.inputs: Arguments: /work/morning and /work/evening notes. Their contents are Tea and Water, each followed by a line break.
teaching.try_change: Change Reading to Menu: and Run again. You should get one heading and the corresponding text per file, in order.

scenarios.title: Publish a safe incident report
scenarios.summary: Combine guards, quoting, filtering and safe output into a reusable script.
scenarios.objective: Create a report from input log $1 at destination $2. If $2 is empty or $1 is not an existing virtual file, print Cannot build report to standard error, exit 2, and leave every file unchanged. Otherwise replace the report with its ERROR lines, print Saved: PATH, and exit 0 even when there are no matches. Valid input and output paths differ.

guide.title: Understand the task
guide.why: Each test starts with its own sample inputs. Simulated files reset before each test. Inspect the inputs and expected results.
guide.action: Use the case selector to inspect inputs, then edit the script.

guide.title: Make the behavior reliable
guide.why: Validation must happen before output redirection: otherwise a failed read can still destroy an old report. No matching incidents is a valid empty report here, so the successful Saved message becomes the final status. Equivalent supported guard structures are accepted.
guide.action: Run script executes every case. Inspect the output and specific failing check, edit, and retry.

guide.title: Explain the edge cases
guide.why: A script that works once can still fail on spaces, missing files or empty data.
guide.action: Compare the cases. Why does the same script handle every input?

scenarios.explanation:
Validation must happen before output redirection: otherwise a failed read can still destroy an old report. No matching incidents is a valid empty report here, so the successful Saved message becomes the final status. Equivalent supported guard structures are accepted.

One supported solution:
if [ -z "$2" ]; then
    printf 'Cannot build report\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
if [ -f "$1" ]; then
    grep -F ERROR "$1" > "$2"
    printf 'Saved: %s\n' "$2"
else
    printf 'Cannot build report\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
hints: Check the destination before using >, which can truncate a file.
Use [ -f "$1" ] to guard the input. An empty destination or missing source must exit before any redirection.
After grep, a successful printf gives status 0 even when grep found no incidents. Consider why that matches this assignment but differs from the previous report task.

teaching.prerequisite_note: Combine labs 1–6: guards, quotes, arguments, output channels, grep and file redirection. The new test here is -f.

concepts.title: Check a file before using it
concepts.text: [ -f "$1" ] succeeds only when argument 1 names an existing ordinary virtual file. It complements -z and -n, which check whether text is empty. A non-empty path can still name a missing file.

concepts.title: Check before changing anything
concepts.text: > creates or clears the output file before reading begins. A missing-input guard must therefore run before the command containing >. The example checks a file and reads it without creating a report; the assignment asks you to combine this with the earlier report-writing skill.

concepts.title: Decide which outcomes are acceptable
concepts.text: grep’s status 1 means no matching lines. For the capstone, an empty report is acceptable: a successful final Saved message can give status 0. A missing input is different; explain that problem on standard error and exit before touching any file.

teaching.example:
if [ -f "$1" ]; then
    cat "$1"
else
    printf 'Input is missing\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
teaching.inputs: Argument 1: /work/greeting. That virtual file contains Welcome, followed by a line break.
teaching.try_change: Change -f to -z and Run again. The path is not empty, so the other branch should run; compare that with checking whether the file exists.
